editorial.text: When you get down to it, public libraries are designed as reusable item-distributors. There’s thousands of them all over the country, often in small neighbourhoods so the public is used to them, with every item barcoded/RFID’d and every borrower carded, with machines dedicated to issue and return. As more and more libraries are discovering, this can be for other items as well as books. Just this week we have the announcement of schemes to lend out musical instruments (Inverclyde), therapeutic light lamps (national scheme), fishing rods and blood pressure monitors (Pennsylvania) and – my favourite – Cards Against Humanity (USA-wide). There’s nothing stopping libraries being used as one-off dropping off/taking places either, with new schemes for unwanted small electricals for recycling being taken (Stirling) and for pads and tampons being given out (Nottingham). The winner overall so far for this sort of thing, though is Devon, with a community fridge, tech donations, explorer backpacks, clothes swaps and seed swaps. That’s not to say that the core business of libraries isn’t books. Books are clearly the main thing and long should they remain so but it’s heartening to see so many people seeing libraries as being available of a lot more besides, especially in this age of concern over the environment and storms rampaging outside. Speaking of the environment, it’s Green Libraries Week in the UK, which focuses on “libraries leading climate and sustainability initiatives for their users and communities.”. The Week is not exactly setting the world alight (to be fair, that’s a bad metaphor) in terms of public awareness but it’s a good starting way of promoting the wonderful things libraries can do. And this is good, for there’s a lot to be said that libraries were the original green institutions, with the reuse of items being central to the business model from the beginning, stretching as far back in ancient Mesopotamia. Friends of the Earth ain’t got nothing on us. So exactly how green are we? Let’s look at the number of books issued in the UK. The DCMS Annual Report 2025/6 estimate 130 million books were issued that year. The only data I can see on the amount of carbon saved per library book issue is from Finland, which says .7kg per issue. So let’s do some math. 130 million x .7 = 91 million kg. Which is great but will mean nothing to most people. So let’s make it visual. Wikipedia gives Richard Osman’s height at 2.01metres. A height calculator suggests a healthy weight for someone that tall is between 74 and 100 kg . Assuming he’s in the middle of that range (he looks healthy to me!) then let’s say 87 kg (13.7 stone). So, let’s err go for a big round number and say libraries save the carbon equivalent of one million Richard Osman’s a year. That’s a good elevator pitch if ever I’ve heard one, especially if you’re talking to Richard Osman. And here’s a GIF I made of it that you can use for free. You’re welcome.
